title: What training does the positive duty under the Sex Discrimination Act expect?
description: What section 47C of the Sex Discrimination Act and the AHRC's Knowledge standard expect of sexual harassment training, who needs it, and what records to keep.
shortAnswer: The positive duty in section 47C of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 requires employers and persons conducting a business or undertaking to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, workplace sexual harassment, sex discrimination and related conduct. The Australian Human Rights Commission's guidelines expect ongoing, role tailored education for all workers, leaders and managers, not one off induction training, supported by records the Commission can assess.
keyTakeaways: Section 47C commenced on 13 December 2022 and applies to all employers and PCBUs, regardless of size.
The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) has had power to inquire into compliance, issue compliance notices and accept enforceable undertakings since 12 December 2023.
The AHRC Guidelines (August 2023) set seven standards; Standard 3, Knowledge, covers policy and education.

The AHRC says one off training at induction has proven ineffective unless it is periodically reinforced, and that education should be tailored to roles such as leaders, board members, HR and those who receive reports.
Suggested records include attendance with a copy of the training content, educational materials, and feedback or survey data on understanding.
appliesTo: Persons conducting a business or undertaking (PCBUs)
Leaders, managers, board members and HR staff with specific roles under the AHRC standards
All workers, including those exposed to third party conduct from customers or clients

sections.heading: What does the positive duty require?

blocks.text: The positive duty requires employers and PCBUs to act proactively to prevent certain unlawful conduct, rather than only responding after a complaint. Section 47C(1) of the [Sex Discrimination Act 1984](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A02868/latest/text) says a duty holder "must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible" the conduct it covers.
The duty covers conduct by the duty holder, its employees or workers, and its agents, namely:

items: sex discrimination that is unlawful in employment and related work areas (sections 14 to 17);
sexual harassment, or harassment on the ground of sex, that is unlawful under section 28B;
conduct creating a workplace environment that is hostile on the ground of sex (section 28M);
victimisation relating to complaints or allegations about any of that conduct.

blocks.text: Section 47C(4) extends the duty to sexual harassment and harassment on the ground of sex directed at employees and workers by any person, which brings third parties such as customers, clients and patients into scope. Section 47C(7) says the duty does not limit duties under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 or state and territory WHS laws, so it operates alongside the psychosocial hazard rules.

The duty was inserted by the Anti Discrimination and Human Rights Legislation Amendment (Respect at Work) Act 2022, and the compilation endnotes record that the relevant items commenced on 13 December 2022. This page reflects the law and AHRC guidance as at September 2026.

sections.heading: What does reasonable and proportionate mean for training?

blocks.text: It means the scale and depth of training depend on the organisation's circumstances, but every duty holder is expected to do something meaningful. Section 47C(6) lists the matters taken into account in deciding compliance.

items: The size, nature and circumstances of the business or undertaking.
The duty holder's resources, whether financial or otherwise.
The practicability and cost of measures to eliminate the conduct.
Any other relevant matter.

blocks.text: A small business may meet the education expectation with a written policy, a short practical session and regular reminders from the owner. A large organisation with higher risk settings, such as customer facing roles, isolated work or alcohol at work events, would be expected to deliver more comprehensive and role specific education. The AHRC [guidance materials](https://humanrights.gov.au/resource-hub/resources-for-organisations-businesses/guidance-materials) include resources for small businesses.

sections.heading: What does the AHRC Knowledge standard say about education and training?

blocks.text: Standard 3 of the AHRC's [Guidelines for Complying with the Positive Duty](https://humanrights.gov.au/__data/assets/file/0030/46974/Guidelines-for-Complying-with-the-Positive-Duty-2023.pdf) expects organisations to develop, communicate and implement a policy on respectful behaviour and unlawful conduct, and to support workers, including leaders and managers, through education. The Commission uses the Guidelines to assess compliance.

The Guidelines are built around seven standards: leadership, culture, knowledge, risk management, support, reporting and response, and monitoring, evaluation and transparency. Under the Knowledge standard, education should cover:

items: expected standards of behaviour, including actions and attitudes that foster equality and respect;
how to identify behaviours that constitute relevant unlawful conduct, and the consequences of engaging in it;
workers' rights and responsibilities for safe, respectful and inclusive workplaces, including their role in preventing and responding to unlawful conduct.

blocks.title: AHRC Guidelines, Standard 3: Knowledge
blocks.text: "Traditional approaches to training and education (for example, one-off training at induction), have proven ineffective at eliminating relevant unlawful conduct, if they are not also periodically reinforced with ongoing opportunities for workers to build and apply their knowledge and skills."

The Guidelines say formal training should be compulsory for all new and existing workers, shown as important by leaders so it is not seen as a "tick-a-box" requirement, led by instructors with expertise in discrimination and harassment, focused on behavioural skills, and interactive. They add that the focus should be on the quality, accessibility and effectiveness of education rather than the frequency of formal sessions, with key concepts revisited over time through training, team meetings and leader messaging. Education should be trauma informed and accessible, including in different formats where needed.

sections.heading: Who needs positive duty training, and how should it differ by role?

blocks.text: Everyone needs baseline education, and specific groups need more. The Guidelines give examples of tailoring education to workers, leaders and managers, senior leaders, board members, HR staff and those responsible for receiving and managing reports.

blocks.text: Mapping content to roles in this way is easier with a [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) that records which outcomes each role must achieve and how they are assessed. The method is set out in [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: What records demonstrate compliance with the Knowledge standard?

blocks.text: The AHRC lists records that might demonstrate the actions taken to meet Standard 3. They show both that education happened and what it contained, which is why a copy of the content matters as much as the attendance list.

items: Attendance records for training sessions or modules, together with a copy of the training content.
Written policies and processes, such as a respectful workplace behaviour policy and reporting procedure.
Notes and agendas from meetings with workers and toolbox talks.
Position descriptions, work plans and performance frameworks with mandatory learning requirements.
Educational materials made available to workers, leaders and managers.
Feedback from workers or engagement survey data showing understanding of, and attitudes towards, relevant unlawful conduct.

blocks.text: The Guidelines also suggest the policy is reviewed regularly, for example annually or after a significant incident, and training content should be reviewed at the same time. A signed [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation) can show that a worker received the policy, but on its own it does not show understanding.

sections.heading: How is the positive duty enforced?

blocks.text: The AHRC enforces the duty through inquiries and compliance tools, with power to act since 12 December 2023. The Guidelines state the Commission can commence an inquiry where it reasonably suspects non compliance, including without the organisation's consent.

items: Conduct inquiries into compliance and make recommendations.
Issue a compliance notice specifying action the organisation must take or stop taking.
Apply to the federal courts for an order directing compliance with a compliance notice.
Enter into enforceable undertakings.

blocks.text: The Commission also has investigative powers to compel information and documents and to examine witnesses. Training records are therefore likely to be among the first documents requested. Separately, following the Guidelines can help an employer show it took all reasonable steps when defending a vicarious liability claim, although that is decided by a court.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures positive duty content as defined concepts, role based learning outcomes and assessment points linked to the AHRC standards and the organisation's own risk assessment. Each item keeps its source and version, so the organisation can show exactly what each audience was taught and assessed on at a given date. See [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence) and [professional services](/industries/professional-services).

faqs.q: Does the positive duty require annual sexual harassment training?
faqs.a: No fixed interval is set in the Act or the Guidelines. The AHRC says the focus should be on the quality, accessibility and effectiveness of education rather than frequency, but it also says one off induction training has proven ineffective unless periodically reinforced. Most organisations combine formal refreshers with ongoing reinforcement through team meetings and leader messaging.

faqs.q: Does the positive duty apply to small businesses?
faqs.a: Yes. It applies to all employers and PCBUs. What is reasonable and proportionate depends on size, resources and the practicability and cost of measures, so a small business can take simpler steps. The AHRC publishes resources aimed at small businesses.

faqs.q: Is an online module enough to meet the Knowledge standard?
faqs.a: An online module can be part of compliance, but the AHRC describes effective education as interactive, skills focused, tailored to roles and reinforced over time. A single online module completed at induction is unlikely to meet that description on its own for a medium or large organisation.

faqs.q: How does the positive duty relate to WHS psychosocial obligations?
faqs.a: Section 47C(7) says the positive duty does not limit WHS duties. Sexual harassment is also a psychosocial hazard under WHS laws, so organisations can design one program that meets both, provided records show how it addresses each set of obligations.

factCheck.claim: Section 47C(1): an employer or PCBU must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, the covered conduct; 47C(2) covers sex discrimination (ss 14 to 17), harassment under s 28B, hostile environments under s 28M and related victimisation.
Section 47C(6) factors: size, nature and circumstances; resources; practicability and cost; any other relevant matter. Section 47C(7) says the duty does not limit WHS duties.
Respect at Work Act 2022 (No. 85, 2022) assented 12 December 2022; compilation endnotes record Schedule 2 items 1 to 13 commencing 13 December 2022.
From 12 December 2023 the Commission has power to enforce compliance: inquiries, compliance notices, court applications to direct compliance, enforceable undertakings.
The Guidelines (August 2023) are centred on seven standards: leadership, culture, knowledge, risk management, support, reporting and response, and monitoring, evaluation and transparency.
Standard 3 states one off training at induction has proven ineffective unless periodically reinforced, and lists records including attendance with a copy of the training content and survey data.
